extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for patent examiners on evaluating claims for subject-matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101 (judicial exceptions, Alice/Mayo framework Steps 2A/2B) and for assessing compliance with the utility requirement (specific, substantial, credible utility). Includes evidentiary standards, handling applicant responses, and record-clarifying practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of a judicial exception at Step 2A
rubrics_metrics.description: When performing the analysis at Step 2A, it is sufficient for the examiner to provide a reasoned rationale that identifies the judicial exception recited in the claim and explains why it is considered a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no requirement for the examiner to rely on evidence, such as publications, to find that a claim is directed to a judicial exception. Examiners may cite relevant case law where courts identified similar exceptions (e.g., Affinity Labs, OIP, Content Extraction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence not required for Step 2B findings but may be used
rubrics_metrics.description: At Step 2B, there is no requirement for evidence to support a finding that the claim does not recite significantly more than the judicial exception (e.g., that additional limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional activities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If available, sources of evidence can support assertions or rebut applicant arguments. Examples: specification statements that elements are conventional, manuals/handbooks showing conventional computer components/functions, patents describing background conventional components, and court decisions. Ensure case-law facts comport with application facts before citing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden shifts to applicant after examiner identifies judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: After examiners identify and explain the reasons why a claim is directed to an abstract idea, natural phenomenon, or law of nature without significantly more, the burden shifts to the applicant to either amend the claim or make a showing why the claim is eligible for patent protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may amend claims (add/modify elements) and/or present persuasive arguments or evidence. Examiners must carefully consider all applicant arguments and evidence rebutting the eligibility rejection and, if claims are amended, determine the amended claim's broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) and redo the eligibility analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to withdraw the rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicant's amendment(s) and/or argument(s) persuasively establish that the claim is not directed to a judicial exception or is directed to significantly more than a judicial exception, the rejection should be withdrawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant can argue that the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more when additional elements are considered both individually and in combination. Examiners must consider both individual and combined effects of added elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: What may qualify as 'significantly more' individually
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional element individually may be enough to qualify as 'significantly more' if it meaningfully limits the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: it improves another technology or technical field; it improves the functioning of a computer itself; it adds well-understood, routine, conventional activity in the field; or it adds unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application. (Note: examiners should be mindful that well-understood/routine/conventional additions ordinarily will not supply 'significantly more' unless they meaningfully limit the exception.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of generic elements can produce 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if an element does not amount to significantly more on its own (e.g., because it is merely a generic computer component performing generic functions), it can still amount to significantly more when considered in combination with other claim elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generic computer components that individually perform generic functions (e.g., CPU performing calculations, clock producing time data) in combination may perform functions that are not generic computer functions and therefore amount to significantly more than an abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling applicant challenges to identification of an abstract idea based on case law
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicant challenges the identification of an abstract idea that was based on a court case and the challenge is not persuasive, the examiner should explain why the abstract idea identified in the claim is similar to the concept in the cited case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the original rejection did not identify a Supreme Court or Federal Circuit decision where a similar abstract idea was found and applicant challenges the identification, the examiner needs to point to such a case and explain why the claim's abstract idea corresponds to that in the case. Adding citation to support the original rationale is not a new ground unless the basic thrust of the rejection changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reevaluation when applicant presents evidence that elements are not conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicant responds to an examiner's assertion that something is well-known, routine, conventional activity with specific argument or evidence that the additional elements are not well-understood/routine/conventional, the examiner should reevaluate whether it is readily apparent that the additional elements are in fact conventional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fully reevaluate when such additional elements are not discussed in the specification as known generic functions/components/activities or are not treated by the courts as conventional. If maintaining rejection, consider providing evidence to support rejection and clarify the record for appeal. See MPEP § 2106.05(d) for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims amended to add generic computer or 'specially programmed' computer
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicant amends a claim to add a generic computer or generic computer components and asserts that the claim recites significantly more because the generic computer is 'specially programmed' or is a 'particular machine', the examiner should evaluate whether the added elements provide significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely adding a generic computer, generic computer components, or a programmed computer to perform generic computer functions does not automatically overcome an eligibility rejection (see Alice and related cases). Examine the actual added functionality and whether it meaningfully limits the exception or is merely conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of preemption arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicant argues that the claim is specific and does not preempt all applications of the exception, the examiner should reconsider Step 2A (is the claim directed to an improvement to the functioning of a computer or to any other technology?) and, if still directed to an exception, reconsider Step 2B (do additional elements amount to an inventive concept?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although preemption is not a standalone test for eligibility, it remains the underlying concern driving the two-part framework from Alice and Mayo. Reconsider both steps with an eye to whether claim scope meaningfully limits the exception and avoids preemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarifying the record when claims are eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: When the claims are deemed patent eligible, the examiner may make clarifying remarks on the record to explain the basis for eligibility or to identify the portion of the specification that describes the claimed improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifying remarks can be made at any point during prosecution, including with a notice of allowance. Examples include noting the specification portion describing the improvement and claim elements producing that improvement, or explaining the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of a claim to assist applicant in responding to rejections (e.g., BRI of a computer-readable-medium claim may cover a carrier wave).

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial claim and specification review for utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Read the claims and the supporting written description to determine what the applicant has claimed, noting any specific embodiments, and ensure the claims define statutory subject matter (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter, or improvement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If at any time it becomes readily apparent that the claimed invention has a well-established utility, do not impose a rejection based on lack of utility. A well-established utility exists if (i) a person of ordinary skill in the art would immediately appreciate why the invention is useful based on the invention's characteristics, and (ii) the utility is specific, substantial, and credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of asserted specific and substantial utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Review the claims and supporting description to determine if the applicant has asserted any specific and substantial utility that is credible for the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant has asserted a credible specific and substantial utility, do not reject for lack of utility. Credibility is assessed from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art in view of the disclosure and any other evidence of record (e.g., test data, declarations, patents, publications). Applicant need only provide one credible assertion for each claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejecting when no credible specific/substantial utility or no well-established utility
rubrics_metrics.description: If no assertion of specific and substantial utility is credible, and the invention does not have a readily apparent well-established utility, reject the claim(s) under 35 U.S.C. 101 for lack of utility and also reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA 112) for failing to teach how to use the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 112 rejection imposed in conjunction with the 101 rejection should incorporate by reference the grounds of the 101 rejection. These rejections shift the burden to the applicant to (i) explicitly identify a specific and substantial utility, and (ii) provide evidence that a POSITA would have recognized that the identified utility was well-established at the time of filing. Ensure an adequate nexus between evidence and properties of the claimed subject matter as disclosed in the application as filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content of a utility rejection (prima facie showing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any rejection based on lack of utility should include a detailed explanation why the claimed invention has no specific and substantial credible utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whenever possible, provide documentary evidence (scientific/technical journals, treatises, patents) to support factual basis for the prima facie showing. If documentary evidence is not available, specifically explain the scientific basis for factual conclusions. The prima facie showing must: (i) clearly set forth reasoning used; (ii) provide support for factual findings; and (iii) evaluate all relevant evidence of record, including utilities taught in the closest prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie showing where asserted utility is not credible
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the asserted specific and substantial utility is not credible, a prima facie showing must establish that it is more likely than not that a person skilled in the art would not consider credible any specific and substantial utility asserted by the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prima facie showing must: (i) explain reasoning for concluding lack of credibility; (ii) support factual findings relied upon; and (iii) evaluate all relevant evidence of record, including closest prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie showing where no specific/substantial utility is disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: Where no specific and substantial utility is disclosed or well-established, a prima facie showing of no specific and substantial utility need only establish that applicant has not asserted a utility and that, on the record before the examiner, there is no known well-established utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain shortcomings and reference absence of evidence showing a well-established utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not maintaining a utility rejection when applicant's assertion is credible
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection based on lack of utility should not be maintained if an asserted utility would be considered specific, substantial, and credible by a person of ordinary skill in the art in view of all evidence of record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel must treat as true a statement of fact made by applicant regarding asserted utility unless countervailing evidence shows a legitimate basis to doubt credibility. Accept qualified expert opinions based on relevant facts whose accuracy is not questioned; do not disregard an opinion solely due to disagreement over significance or meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's burden to rebut a prima facie utility rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a proper prima facie showing of no specific and substantial credible utility has been established, the applicant bears the burden of rebutting it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may rebut by amending claims, providing reasoning/arguments, or submitting evidence (declarations under 37 CFR 1.132, patents, printed publications). Examiners should review original disclosure, evidence relied upon, claim amendments, and any new reasoning/evidence, and must recognize, fully consider, and respond to each substantive element of the applicant's response. If rebuttal is satisfactory, withdraw the 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection and the corresponding 35 U.S.C. 112 rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific utility standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'specific utility' is specific to the subject matter claimed and provides a well-defined and particular benefit to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish specific uses from general utility statements. Examples of insufficient specificity: indicating a compound may be useful in treating unspecified disorders, describing a polynucleotide merely as a 'gene probe' without a specific DNA target, or general diagnostic utility without identifying the condition. Assertions that reasonably correlate a disclosed biological activity to a disease condition can be sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial utility standard
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Substantial utility' requires the asserted use to show a significant and presently available benefit to the public; utilities that require further research to identify or confirm a real-world context are not substantial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples that are not substantial utilities include: basic research into properties/mechanisms, methods to treat unspecified diseases, assays that identify materials having no specific/substantial utility, methods of making materials that lack utility, and claims to intermediate products intended for making a final product that lacks utility. Do not require that products/services be currently available to the public; any reasonable use that provides a public benefit is acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research tools can satisfy utility if specific and substantial
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions used in research/laboratory settings (research tools) can have clear, specific, and substantial utility (e.g., gas chromatographs, screening assays).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not label an invention as lacking utility solely because it is for research use. Focus on whether the asserted utility requires further research to identify or confirm a real-world use. Labels like 'research tool,' 'intermediate,' or 'for research purposes' are not determinative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wholly inoperative inventions and 'incredible' utility
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention that is 'inoperative' (does not operate to produce the results claimed) is not 'useful' under patent law; however, to violate 35 U.S.C. 101 the claimed device must be totally incapable of achieving a useful result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A small degree of utility is sufficient; partial success is sufficient to demonstrate patentable utility. An invention does not lack utility merely because an embodiment performs crudely, is imperfect, or does not operate under all conditions. The defense of non-utility requires proof of total incapacity.
